steps.title: The rule: Separating transport, testable business logic and persistence responsibilities

blocks.text: A dependency can extract reusable input-provision logic from individual operation handlers and expose the supplied value as a declared handler parameter.

Transport handlers adapt HTTP inputs and outputs, business callables enforce application rules, and persistence adapters access stored state; separate these responsibilities so each can change without embedding the other responsibilities. Move a business decision from a handler into a plain callable with explicit inputs, keep the HTTP adaptation in the handler, and call a separate persistence adapter for stored state rather than treating separate files alone as a responsibility boundary.

edges.label: stored-state access; not embedded in handler

blocks.alt_text: Make the order flow visible across three responsibility boundaries: HTTP adaptation in the handler, the order decision in a plain business callable, and stored-state access in a persistence adapter. Show reusable input provisioning entering through a declared handler parameter, and distinguish responsibility boundaries from file boundaries.

steps.title: Trace the boundary: Separating transport, testable business logic and persistence responsibilities

blocks.text: Keep HTTP adaptation in the handler, the order decision in a plain callable with explicit inputs, and stored-state access in a persistence adapter. A dependency can supply reusable input provisioning through a declared handler parameter. Separate responsibilities, not just files: moving the same mixture into several modules does not establish those boundaries.

steps.title: The rule: Bounded in-process background work and nondurable delivery limits

blocks.text: Declare a BackgroundTasks handler parameter and call background_tasks.add_task(callable, *args, **kwargs) to schedule work after sending the response.

A background task callable can be a normal def or async def function; FastAPI handles either form. BackgroundTasks work runs in the application process and cannot guarantee survival or delivery when that process fails.

nodes.label: Follow-up task: def or async def

edges.label: pending work can be lost; no guaranteed survival or delivery

blocks.alt_text: Show an order handler registering follow-up work, sending its response, and then running the task inside the application-process boundary. Mark a process failure after the response as a point where pending work can be lost, separating response delivery from follow-up completion.

steps.title: Trace the boundary: Bounded in-process background work and nondurable delivery limits

blocks.text: Declare BackgroundTasks and register a callable with background_tasks.add_task(callable, *args, **kwargs). The response is sent before follow-up work runs in the application process. The callable may use def or async def. If the process fails, survival or delivery cannot be guaranteed. Scheduling therefore does not prove durable completion.

steps.title: Bounded in-process background work and nondurable delivery limits

segments.label: Deferred email work and the risk of losing pending tasks
segments.summary: Sending email can delay a response while the application communicates with an email server. FastAPI background tasks let the response go first and the email work run afterward. Pending tasks are lost if the server crashes. Work requiring guaranteed delivery needs a different execution arrangement. The example treats a password-reset email as acceptable to defer because the user can request another.

blocks.group_title: Response-first work and the process-failure boundary

bridge.before: Watch for the response-first sequence and the loss of pending work on a server crash. The clip's email example assumes requesting another email is acceptable; suitability depends on the operation's required outcome.
bridge.after: The clip explains the delivery limitation but omits the handler parameter, add_task syntax, and supported callable forms. The text supplies those details and makes the application-process boundary explicit.

steps.title: The rule: Composing request dependency graphs

blocks.text: A provider can declare its own Annotated[Type, Depends(other_provider)] parameter, forming a dependency graph.

FastAPI resolves a provider's prerequisite inputs before calling that provider and supplies its result to the consuming operation. A sub-dependency can declare typed query inputs of its own; those inputs are extracted from the request before its returned value is supplied to the dependent provider.

nodes.label: Typed page and page_size query inputs

edges.label: resolve prerequisite and supply its result

blocks.alt_text: Make the dependency direction and execution order visible: typed page and page_size request inputs → pagination provider → order-options provider → consuming operation.

steps.title: Trace the boundary: Composing request dependency graphs

blocks.text: The pagination provider declares typed page and page_size query inputs. FastAPI extracts those inputs and resolves pagination before supplying its result to order-options; the consuming operation then receives the order-options result. A provider declares a prerequisite with Annotated[Type, Depends(other_provider)]. Trace from prerequisites toward consumers, not the reverse.

b.message: A consumer needs its prerequisites resolved first.

blocks.text: Separate files alone are not separate concerns. Responsibilities must be separated so one can change without embedding the others.
Adding a background task does not prove that it survives process failure or delivers its effect. In-process scheduling is not durable completion.
A provider does not run before its unresolved prerequisite inputs are available. Resolve the graph from prerequisites to consumers.
